### Question 1

Think of the meaningful word parts as train cars and the combining vowel as the coupler between them. The coupler carries no cargo, but without it the cars would slam together into something unpronounceable like "gastrenterlogy." Drop an o between them and you get gastroenterology, which your mouth can actually manage. So when a long term lands in front of you, mentally pull out the couplers and read the cargo: gastr (stomach), enter (small intestine), logy (study of).

### Question 2

Attach an image to each prefix and it stops being a memorization chore. Brady is a sloth: whatever follows is happening slowly, so bradycardia is a slow heart and bradypnea is slow breathing. Tachy is the roadrunner on the opposite side of the same pair. Build a few of these opposing pairs (brady/tachy for speed, hypo/hyper for amount, poly/oligo for number) and you can decode dozens of terms without opening a dictionary.

### Question 3

Read a medical word from the back, the way you open a package from the label end. The suffix is the label that tells you what was done. When the label reads -ectomy, think "exit": something was taken out, so an appendectomy means the appendix left the body. If the label reads -scopy instead, nothing was removed at all; a clinician simply looked inside with a scope. Same organ, completely different day for the patient.

### Question 4

The combining vowel is a bridge, and you only build a bridge where there is a gap. The suffix -megaly starts with the consonant m, so the root and suffix would collide; the o smooths the landing. The suffix -itis already starts with a vowel, so the gap is closed and adding an o would give you the clunky "hepatoitis." One exception worth memorizing: between two roots the bridge always stays, vowel or not, which is why gastroenteritis keeps its o.

### Question 5

Picture a wall. An -otomy cuts a slit in it, and the slit is closed again at the end of the operation. An -ostomy cuts an opening and installs a doorway that stays open afterward, sometimes only until the bowel heals and a surgeon goes back in to reverse it, sometimes for life. An -ectomy takes the wall out entirely. The extra s in -ostomy is your cue: it points to stoma, the Greek word for mouth or opening, which is exactly the doorway that remains. What the suffix does not tell you is how long that doorway lasts, so read on for words like temporary, diverting, or permanent.

### Question 6

Some terms are recipe cards: osteoarthritis literally spells out bone-joint-inflammation, so you can assemble the meaning yourself from parts you already know. Others are street signs named after the mayor. Parkinson Street tells you nothing about what stands on it, and no amount of decoding will help. That second kind is an eponym. The practical move is to sort new vocabulary into those two bins as you read: decode the recipe cards, and simply memorize the street signs.

### Question 7

These words kept the plural endings of the languages they came from, and each ending has its own switch. Learn them as a short list of swaps: -um to -a (bacterium, bacteria), -us to -i (nucleus, nuclei), -is to -es (diagnosis, diagnoses), -ix or -ex to -ices (appendix, appendices), -a to -ae (vertebra, vertebrae), -on to -a (phenomenon, phenomena). The usual trap is not forgetting a swap but grabbing the wrong one, like giving a word that ends in -us the ending that belongs to -um.

### Question 8

This sentence gives you two independent sets of clues, and either one alone gets you most of the way. Word parts crack dyspnea: dys means difficult, -pnea means breathing. Then the connector although works like a seesaw, so whatever exertion did to the symptom, rest did the opposite. Since exacerbated pushed it up, abated must have brought it down. Notice how close dyspnea sits to dysphagia (-phagia, swallowing), which is exactly why careful readers slow down on the middle of a term.

### Question 9

Two words that sound alike and sit one vowel apart need a hook. Use the vowel itself: ilEum goes with intEstine, ilIum goes with hIp. Then confirm with context rather than the hook alone. The cecum is the first pouch of the large intestine, so whatever empties into it has to be part of the gut, which settles the spelling as ileum. Homophone pairs like this are the reason careful readers slow down on the vowel instead of skimming the shape of a word.

### Question 10

Researchers build their confidence level into the sentence itself, the way a forecaster says "seventy percent chance of rain" instead of "it will rain." Suggest and association mean "these two things showed up together in our data more than we would expect"; they do not mean "one produced the other." Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together every summer, but the ice cream is not burning anyone; the sun is doing both jobs. Find the hedge word first, and you will read the claim at the strength the authors intended.

### Question 11

In everyday speech significant means big; in research it means unlikely to be a fluke, and those are separate questions. Picture a coin weighted so slightly you would never notice it. Flip it a million times and it lands heads 50.4 percent of the time. With that many flips, a 0.4 point edge is far too consistent to be luck, so it is statistically significant, yet the edge is small enough that it would never change a single game. Significance answers "is it real?" You still have to look up the effect size to answer "is it big enough to matter?"

### Question 12

Take the word apart from the back, like unstacking blocks. The top block, -penia, means too few. Below it, cyt means cell. At the bottom, thromb means clot. Restack the meanings and you have too few clot cells, which are the platelets, the tiny patches that plug a damaged vessel. Fewer patches means easy bruising and prolonged bleeding, and you predicted the clinical picture without ever looking the word up. Swap only the top block and you get a different diagnosis: -osis gives too many, -megaly gives too large.
